ideas.hypothesis: The yield-curve spread predicts regional recessions less well the more specialized a region's production structure is: the 12-month-ahead predictive power of the term spread for regional recession probabilities falls as a region's industrial specialization index rises, because specialized regions have more asymmetric, idiosyncratic cycles.

sources.role: method: probit model of recessions on the long-short interest rate spread
finding: the term structure is the most reliable financial leading indicator across countries
method/measure: Kim-Nelson plucking-model Markov-switching filter giving regional recession probabilities and a regional cycle chronology
mechanism/measure: specialization in production drives asymmetry of regional fluctuations; specialization index

ideas.test: Use quarterly real output or coincident indices for US states (or Canadian provinces), about 1980-2019. Estimate regional recession probabilities with a plucking-type Markov-switching model. Run a panel probit of the regional recession indicator on the national 10y-3m spread lagged 4 quarters, interacted with each region's pre-sample Krugman specialization index built from sectoral employment shares. Compare pseudo-R2 and AUROC by specialization tercile.
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction between spread and specialization is zero or positive, or the spread's AUROC is similar across specialization terciles.

ideas.hypothesis: In an agriculture- and export-heavy state economy, the survey-based business-expectations component of a state leading index adds out-of-sample predictive power for six-month-ahead state employment growth beyond the hard-data components (permits, airline passengers, manufacturing hours, UI claims, dollar), and the gain is concentrated around turning points.

sources.role: measure: LEI-N composition (six components incl. Survey of Nebraska Business expectations) and its six-month-ahead target
setting: Nebraska business-conditions reporting series
finding/setting: regional business outlook surveys signalling turns in the Ninth District

ideas.test: Collect monthly LEI-N component series and Nebraska nonfarm payroll employment (BLS CES), about 2005-2019. Using rolling-origin forecasts, compare RMSE of 6-month-ahead employment growth from a model with hard components only versus one adding the survey expectations component. Evaluate separately for months within 6 months of state turning points dated by a Markov-switching model.
ideas.disconfirming: Adding the survey component does not reduce out-of-sample RMSE overall or near turning points (Diebold-Mariano test not significant).

ideas.hypothesis: Business-cycle co-movement between Nebraska and Texas depends on which commodity shock dominates: their cycles are more synchronized when agricultural price shocks dominate and less synchronized when oil price shocks dominate, because Nebraska's cycle tracks its farm cycle while Texas is energy-exposed.

sources.role: finding/mechanism: Nebraska's cycle tied to its agricultural cycle and only weakly to the national cycle
setting: Texas business reviews tracking cotton and sectoral conditions
setting: Texas business situation and construction indicators
measure: Nebraska leading indicator components, including export/dollar exposure

ideas.test: Use the Philadelphia Fed state coincident indices for Nebraska and Texas, monthly 1980-2019. Compute 24-month rolling correlations of growth rates. Regress the rolling correlation on the rolling share of variance in a crop price index versus WTI oil price, controlling for national coincident index volatility.
ideas.disconfirming: The Nebraska-Texas correlation is unrelated to, or moves opposite to, the relative importance of agricultural versus oil price shocks.

ideas.hypothesis: Austrian industrial business conditions respond with a 1-2 month lag to sentiment in the German automotive sector, and this cross-border confidence spillover predicts Austrian industrial production growth beyond domestic indicators and world trade.

sources.role: finding: Austrian upswing driven by exports; sentiment indicators foreshadow moderation
mechanism: Austrian industry assessments linked to German auto sector stabilisation and world trade
method: large regular business survey of a small open regional economy
measure: business outlook survey readings as indicators of conditions

ideas.test: Monthly WIFO business survey (industry assessments), ifo business climate for German automotive manufacturing, Austrian industrial production index, and a world trade volume index (CPB), 1996-2019. Estimate a VAR or local projections and Granger tests of whether German auto sentiment predicts Austrian industrial assessments and output, controlling for world trade and Austrian lags.
ideas.disconfirming: German automotive sentiment carries no predictive content for Austrian industrial assessments or production once world trade and domestic lags are controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: As the Mises-Hayek credit-expansion theory predicts, periods when the policy rate sits below an estimated natural rate expand early-stage, long-duration sectors (construction, capital goods) relative to consumer-goods sectors, and the subsequent contraction is deeper in those same sectors. A monetarist view instead predicts roughly uniform sectoral effects.

sources.role: mechanism: Austrian (Mises/Rothbard/Hayek) vs monetarist accounts of credit over-expansion and the bank lending decision
mechanism: Lachmann's subjectivist expectations and the role of institutions in coordination
method: Lutz's call for models identifying which disturbing factors cause specific crises rather than assuming generic waves

ideas.test: Use US industry-level real output or investment (BEA GDP by industry / Fed industrial production by stage of processing), 1965-2019, with a natural rate estimate (Laubach-Williams). Run local projections of the capital-goods/construction output share relative to consumer goods on the lagged policy-rate gap, and test whether the cumulative boom response is followed by a larger bust in the same sectors.
ideas.disconfirming: The policy-rate gap has no differential effect on early-stage versus consumer-goods sectors, or the effects are symmetric with no subsequent sector-specific reversal.

ideas.hypothesis: Including a business-survey expectations component in a state leading indicator lowers the false-signal rate (single-month declines not followed by slowdowns) compared with an index built only from hard data.

sources.role: finding/measure: LEI-N single-month reversals (July 2013 decline after June rise) and survey component
setting: state business reporting that publishes survey and indicator data
setting: later issue of the same series providing additional monthly readings

ideas.test: Reconstruct monthly LEI-N variants with and without the Survey of Nebraska Business component, 2005-2019. Define signals as declines larger than a threshold. Count signals followed and not followed within 6 months by a slowdown in state employment growth. Compare false-positive and hit rates.
ideas.disconfirming: The index with the survey component has an equal or higher false-signal rate, or a lower hit rate, than the hard-data-only index.

ideas.hypothesis: Firms' expected sales in state business outlook surveys predict six-month-ahead growth in state net taxable retail sales, with stronger predictive power in rural counties where retail spending depends on agricultural income.

sources.role: measure: survey respondents' six-month-ahead sales and employment expectations
mechanism/measure: agricultural cycle drives the state economy; net taxable retail sales as a state indicator
setting: business review and prospect reporting in a farm state economy
measure: retail sales tracked as a cyclical indicator in regional business reviews

ideas.test: Monthly Survey of Nebraska Business expected-sales balance and Nebraska Department of Revenue net taxable retail sales by county, 2005-2019. Run a county panel regression of 6-month-ahead retail sales growth on the survey balance, interacted with county farm-income share (BEA CAINC), with county fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The survey balance does not predict retail sales growth, or its predictive power does not differ between rural agricultural and urban counties.

ideas.hypothesis: The spread between firms' forward-looking outlook (expected sales) and their current confidence or assessment of conditions is systematically over-optimistic late in expansions, and a widening spread predicts a regional slowdown within two quarters.

sources.role: method/data: large regular business survey separating current conditions and expectations
finding: business outlook reaching multi-year highs as a cyclical signal
setting: regional business conditions publication
measure: expectations of sales and employment over the next six months

ideas.test: Quarterly Scottish Chambers' Business Survey balances (current trends versus expected trends), 1998-2019, and Scottish GDP growth. Compute the expectations-minus-current spread. Test whether realized forecast errors vary by cycle phase, and whether the spread predicts GDP growth deceleration two quarters ahead in a probit.
ideas.disconfirming: Forecast errors show no phase dependence and the spread has no predictive power for subsequent slowdowns.

ideas.hypothesis: Regional business survey balances predict turning points in the Texas economy earlier than hard data, and the lead is longer for manufacturing respondents with more export exposure than for services respondents.

sources.role: method: design and scale of a regional chambers business survey
setting: Texas business situation and construction trends
setting: comparable state business-conditions reporting

ideas.test: Monthly Dallas Fed Texas Business Outlook Surveys (manufacturing and services general activity indexes), 2004-2019, and the Texas coincident index. Run Granger causality tests and turning-point lead analysis (Bry-Boschan dates) separately for manufacturing and services indexes, controlling for lagged payroll employment.
ideas.disconfirming: Survey indexes add no predictive power beyond lagged hard data, or the manufacturing index shows no longer lead than services.

ideas.hypothesis: Business confidence in Nebraska is driven more by farm income and crop prices than by national confidence, so state-specific confidence shocks have smaller and shorter-lived employment effects than in diversified states.

sources.role: method: regional business confidence survey design
setting: Nebraska business conditions data

ideas.test: Monthly Survey of Nebraska Business expectations, 2005-2019, regressed on USDA Nebraska farm income or a crop price index and on national CEO/business confidence (Conference Board). Then estimate a state VAR of employment on confidence and compare impulse responses with a diversified-state benchmark.
ideas.disconfirming: National confidence explains more variance in Nebraska business confidence than farm income, or confidence shocks have effects as persistent as in diversified states.
